opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the term comes originally from Donald Campbell, the evolutionary epistemologist. His idea was that in any evolutionary process you have variation and selection, but often the selection isn't done directly by the environment killing off the losers. Instead you get proxies, internal mechanisms that anticipate what the environment would select for and do the selecting in advance. Vision is a nice example: rather than an organism bumping into things and dying, it can see the cliff and avoid it. The eye is doing selection vicariously, on behalf of the environment.

I find this a really useful lens for thinking about technological development and especially about the kind of soft technological determinism I've been interested in. A naive picture of competition says that societies adopt various technologies and institutions, then the ones that are less competitive militarily or economically get conquered or outcompeted, and over time you see this ruthless filtering. That does happen historically. But much more often, what you see is actors anticipating that pressure. A state looks at its neighbours, sees that they're industrialising or building a certain kind of military, and concludes, "If we don't do this, we'll be in trouble." So they adopt it before the selection pressure ever bites directly. Firms do the same thing when they look at where markets are going.

The implication is that competitive dynamics can be much more powerful and much faster than you'd expect if you only counted actual cases of societies being eliminated. You might say, "Very few countries actually got wiped out for failing to adopt some technology, so competition must be weak." But that misses that the threat is internalised. Decision-makers are running the simulation in their heads, and it shapes behaviour long before any losses occur.

For AI, I think this matters a lot. Much of the pressure to race, to deploy quickly, and to integrate AI into militaries and economies operates through this anticipatory channel. Leaders worry about falling behind, and that worry drives the trajectory. The good news is that vicarious selection runs on beliefs and models of the world, so in principle it's more steerable than brute environmental selection. If you can change how actors perceive the stakes, for instance by showing that certain kinds of development are dangerous to everyone or that cooperation is verifiable and stable, you can change what gets selected. The bad news is that mistaken or exaggerated beliefs about competition can be self-fulfilling, and that can lock in dynamics nobody actually wanted.

r001.rationale: It contrasts direct environmental elimination with internal mechanisms that anticipate what the environment would select, and describes decision-makers running a simulation in their heads before pressure bites.

r002.rationale: It links technology adoption to anticipated military and economic competition, but does not describe model-based technological experimentation as a selection process nested within that competition.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it, vicarious selection is a concept that comes out of the evolutionary and cultural evolution literature, and it's really useful for understanding how technology develops in a way that doesn't require any single actor to have a full picture of what's going on.

The basic idea is this. In biological evolution, selection operates directly: organisms with certain traits survive and reproduce, and those that don't, don't. It's brutal and it's slow. Vicarious selection is when some process stands in for that direct selection, a proxy that lets you select among variants without having to actually run the full, costly, sometimes fatal experiment. So your brain, in a sense, is a vicarious selection mechanism. You can imagine jumping off a cliff, simulate the outcome, and reject that option without having to do it. Your thinking does the selecting on behalf of the world.

When you apply that to technology, what you see is that a lot of what looks like deliberate, intelligent design is actually layered selection processes. There's the market, which selects among products that firms produce. There are firms, which internally select among projects and prototypes. There are engineers, who select among designs in their heads. And then there's science and theory, which lets you anticipate which designs could even work before you build them. Each of those layers is vicarious with respect to the one below it: it's doing some of the selecting that would otherwise have to happen through expensive real-world failure.

And the reason I find this framing important, especially for thinking about AI and other powerful technologies, is that it reframes the question of control. We often talk as if the key question is whether humans are "in charge" of where technology goes. But under the vicarious selection view, a lot of the direction of technology is set by the structure of the selection environment, not by anyone's intentions. Military competition selects for certain capabilities. Economic competition selects for others. Individual designers are, in a sense, just generating variation that these larger environments then filter.

So when people ask, "Could we just choose not to build a dangerous technology?", the vicarious selection lens says: well, it depends on what the selection environment rewards. If there's a strong competitive gradient pulling toward that technology, then individual restraint is a variation that tends to get selected out. That's the pessimistic reading.

But there's an optimistic reading too, which is that we can deliberately shape the selection environment. We can build institutions, norms, agreements, evaluation regimes, that act as new vicarious selection layers. If we can get good at anticipating consequences, through forecasting, through red-teaming, through evals in the AI context, then we can do more of the selecting in our heads and our institutions, rather than letting the world do it for us the hard way. That's really the whole project of technology governance, in my view: inserting better vicarious selection upstream of the irreversible stuff.

And I'd add one caveat, which is that it's genuinely hard to know how much selection is happening at each layer. Historically I think we've overrated the role of individual foresight and underrated the role of competition and path dependence. So part of the discipline is being honest about which layer is actually steering, and then asking what it would take to change that.

r001.rationale: It explains that people can simulate an action’s outcome and reject it without carrying out the costly real-world experiment.

r002.rationale: It describes engineers, firms, and science using internal or theoretical selection before real-world testing, with markets and economic competition selecting among the resulting products and capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think of vicarious selection as selection that happens through a proxy for the pressures that ultimately determine success. Instead of having to build every possible technology and see which ones survive in the world, we can select among designs in our heads, in simulations, or through small experiments.

An engineer can look at a bridge design and say, “That’s going to collapse,” and discard it without actually building the bridge. In that sense, the engineer’s judgment is standing in for the selection pressure that gravity would otherwise exert. That’s an enormous advantage: we can learn without paying the full cost of failure.

But the important question is how well the proxy captures what we actually care about. If we select technologies for profitability, or military advantage, those pressures may be quite effective at producing certain capabilities without selecting for safety or social benefit. So understanding technological development requires looking both at the ultimate pressures and at the judgments, tests, and institutions that anticipate them—and sometimes get them wrong.

r001.rationale: It explains that designs can be selected through thought, simulations, or small experiments instead of building every technology and testing it in the world.

r002.rationale: It names profitability as a possible selection pressure, but does not describe model-based experimentation as nested within broader economic competition.

sol-6.1.text:
Vicarious selection is when selection happens on a representation of something, rather than on the thing itself. So instead of building ten bridges and finding out which ones collapse, you build models of those bridges, test them, and then construct the one you expect to work best. The models undergo selection on behalf of the actual bridges.

And a lot of technological development works this way. We can try out ideas in our heads, in drawings, in simulations, or in laboratory experiments. That allows us to explore alternatives much more cheaply than if we had to build and deploy every technology and see what happened.

But the crucial question is whether the criteria we're using in that process actually track what we care about. A design might perform very well in a simulation and fail in the real world because the simulation left something out. So vicarious selection gives us an enormous capacity to anticipate and direct technological change, but its success depends on how well our representations capture the consequences that matter.

r001.rationale: It defines vicarious selection as testing representations or models of bridges instead of building and trialing the bridges themselves.

r002.rationale: It describes model-based technological experimentation but does not place that selection process within broader economic competition.
